newsitem.title: UK: Scottish nationalists to camapign for devolution.
newsitem.headline: Scottish nationalists to camapign for devolution.

text.p: The Scottish National Party said on Sunday it would campaign for a "yes" vote in a referendum on a Scottish parliament.
Britain's new Labour government on Thursday announced plans for Scotland to have its first parliament for 300 years, provided five million Scots back the idea in a referendum on September 11.
The parliament will have tax-raising powers when it starts sitting in the year 2000, but government ministers insist it will not usher in independence.
But leaders of the Scottish National Party, which wants independence for Scotland, decided that devolution is not an obstacle to an independent state.
The party's executive committee at a meeting in Edinburgh unanimously approved a recommendation from SNP leader Alec Salmond to campaign for a devolved Scottish parliament.
"I think it is a step forward, a modest step forward," Salmond told reporters. "I think it is in the best interests of the people of Scotland."
The SNP's national council meets next week to endorse the decision.

The establishment of subsidiary, or devolved, parliaments for Sotland and Wales was a key part of Labour's plans to reform Britain's centralised constitution that helped the party sweep to power in a May 1 election.
The new Scottish body would be the first legislative authority north of the border since the 1707 Act of Union, which brought together the kingdoms of Scotland and England.

The new 129-member assembly, to be elected, unlike its London equivalent, by a system of proportional representation, would make laws in many areas and administer education, health care, environment, agriculture and arts policies.

Foreign and defence policy, the economic and monetary system, employment legislation, social security and certain sensitive areas such as abortion, broadcasting and gambling would continue to be dealt with by the London government.
Labour has proposed a similar, but much less powerful, assembly for Wales.
Welsh and Scottish voters were told on Sunday that if they approved plans for their own parliaments, a Conservative government in London would not abolish them if it returned to power.
Conservative Party leader William Hague said his party was still opposed to devolution.
"In Scotland and Wales we believe it would be a fundamental mistake to set up parliaments which could break up the United Kingdom," he told BBC radio.
"If they vote for it in the referendums then they will get a Scottish parliament and a Welsh assembly. We will have to respect that in the future."
In the May election, the Conservatives lost all their seats in Wales and Scotland.
